say: You give it a rule, a mapping or a graph. It tells you whether it is a **function**, and names its domain, codomain and range.
The key idea: a function gives every input exactly **one** output. An input with two arrows leaving it breaks the rule.
what.out: function or not; domain and range

example.question: A mapping is given by $f(x) = 2x - 1$, with domain $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ and codomain $\mathbb{N}$. Show that $f$ is a function and write down its range.

steps.title: Find each output
steps.say: A function needs exactly one output for every input. Work out the output for each number in the domain.

steps.title: Say why it is a function
steps.say: Look at what you found. Every input has one output and no input has two, so the rule holds.

lines.text: Each input has exactly one output, so $f$ is a function.

steps.title: Name the range
steps.say: The **range** is the set of outputs the rule actually produces. The codomain, $\mathbb{N}$, is the larger set they are allowed to land in. List only the outputs you found.

lines.text: The range is smaller than the codomain: $2$ and $4$ are in $\mathbb{N}$ but are never hit.

say: You give it a function, $f(x)$, and an input. The input can be a number or an expression. It gives back the **output**.
The key idea: wherever you see $x$ in the rule, write the input in its place, inside brackets, then simplify.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as the opening 5-mark part of long Paper 1 questions: put a number into a given formula (a cost, a height, a proportion) and give the answer with the right rounding or unit, before calculus or logs take over.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks it nearly every year on Paper 1, as the first part of a 50-mark function question: substitute a time or an amount into a given formula, or fill a table of values to draw a graph.

example.question: $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 5$. (i) Find $f(-3)$. (ii) Find $f(a+1)$ in terms of $a$.

steps.title: Substitute the number
steps.say: Replace every $x$ with $-3$. Put $-3$ in brackets so the minus sign is squared too.

steps.title: Work out part (i)
steps.say: Square first, then multiply, then add.

steps.title: Substitute the expression
steps.say: This time the input is $a + 1$. Replace every $x$ with the whole bracket $(a + 1)$.

steps.title: Expand and collect
steps.say: Expand $(a+1)^2$ and $-4(a+1)$, then collect like terms.

higher.tip: On a short first part the substitution is where the marks sit. Write it out: some correct substitution earns partial credit even if the arithmetic then goes wrong.
Round as the question asks. An answer with incorrect rounding or no rounding loses a mark.
Give the unit when the question has one. A correct answer with no unit or the wrong unit loses a mark.
A correct answer with no working still gets full marks on these parts, but a wrong one with no working gets nothing, so show the substitution.

ordinary.tip: Writing the number into the formula earns marks even if the answer is wrong: the scheme gives credit for substituting the value in.

sources.quote: substitutes in the 15 to the given formula

ordinary.tip: When a part asks what your answer means, say it in words and with the unit: the scheme gives marks for the explanation.

sources.quote: Work of merit in the explanation

ordinary.tip: Leaving off the unit does not cost you here, but a correct answer needs to be exact: show the value of the formula, not just a rounded guess.
If you are stuck on a later part, writing the value you found in the part before still earns credit.

sources.quote: Accept correct answer without supporting work

say: You give it a linear rule, $ax + b$, and a domain. It gives you the **straight-line** graph.
The key idea: two points fix a line. Find two (a third checks you), plot them and join them with a ruler.

how.higher: Higher level asks it as a plotting part on Paper 1, worth 5 to 15 marks: complete a table or find two points on a line such as $y = 12 - (2+\pi)x$, then plot and join them over the stated domain.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks it on both papers, worth 5 to 15 marks: draw a line from its rule or from a slope and a point, over a stated domain, and then read something off the graph.

example.question: Draw the graph of $f(x) = 2x - 1$ for $-1 \le x \le 3$.

steps.title: Choose some x-values
steps.say: Two points fix a straight line. Take the two ends of the domain and a third point in between to check.

steps.title: Write the table
steps.say: Pair each $x$ with its $y$. These are the points to plot.

steps.title: Plot and join
steps.say: Plot the three points. They should sit on one line. Join them with a **ruler**, starting at $x = -1$ and stopping at $x = 3$.

lines.text: The line slopes up by $2$ for every $1$ across and crosses the $y$-axis at $-1$, matching $2x - 1$.

higher.tip: Draw with a ruler. A freehand graph loses a mark.
Finding two points on the line is worth high partial credit before you even draw it, so write them down first.
Stay inside the stated domain. A line plotted correctly but not graphed in the stated domain loses a mark.

ordinary.tip: Use a ruler. A line not drawn with a ruler loses a mark.

sources.quote: Line not drawn with a ruler

ordinary.tip: Draw the line over the whole domain given. A line drawn in a reduced domain loses a mark.
Finding a second point is credited as work of merit even if the line is not finished.

say: You give it a function, $f(x)$, and a value $a$ to approach. It tells you the **limiting value** $f(x)$ closes in on, even if $f(a)$ itself is not allowed.
The key idea: do not put in $a$. Try $x$ values closer and closer to $a$ from below and from above. If both sides head for the same number, that number is the limit.

how.higher: Higher level has tested it once, as a 5-mark Paper 1 part asking what a cooling-temperature formula settles down to as time goes on, to be described in words.

example.question: $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}$. Explain why $f(3)$ cannot be found. Complete a table for $x$ close to $3$ on each side and write down the limit of $f(x)$ as $x \to 3$.

steps.title: See the problem at 3
steps.say: Try $x = 3$ first. The top and the bottom both become $0$, and $\tfrac{0}{0}$ has no value. So go as close to $3$ as you can instead.

steps.title: Come from below
steps.say: Choose values just under $3$ and work out $f(x)$ for each.

steps.title: Read the limit
steps.say: From both sides the values close in on $\hl{1}{6}$. That number is the limit.

lines.text: Check: $x^2 - 9 = (x-3)(x+3)$, so $f(x) = x + 3$ for $x \ne 3$, and that is $6$ at $x = 3$.

higher.tip: When asked what a limit means in context, any valid description scores. Name the quantity, for example the lowest temperature the coffee will cool to.

sources.quote: The lowest temperature the coffee will cool to

higher.tip: Even a partial answer earns marks if it mentions the quantity or the word limit.
